scale: 0-10 integer, NA if the text gives no evidence bearing on the criterion
task: Each entry is a candidate criterion for judging machine-learning conference paper abstracts. Classify each as quality-relevant or incidental.

criteria.name: Discriminative evaluation — designed to decide between hypotheses, not to demonstrate the method
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge whether the abstract poses a question with more than one possible answer, and separately whether the reported evaluation is structured to distinguish those answers (comparisons that could have come out the other way, ablations that isolate a cause); score 0-10 for the two TOGETHER. Score low when the evaluation exists only to show the proposal wins.

criteria.name: Belief-change — the output is a changed understanding rather than a delivered artifact
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the main thing a reader takes away is a revised belief about how something works, as opposed to a tool, model, or dataset they can now use. Both are legitimate contributions; score only which one the abstract is offering.

criteria.name: Cost stated TOGETHER WITH gain, so the trade is checkable
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge whether the abstract quantifies what its method gains, and separately whether it quantifies what the method costs (compute, latency, accuracy given up, extra passes); score 0-10 for BOTH being given in commensurable terms, so a reader could decide whether the trade is worth taking.

criteria.name: Limiting result stated TOGETHER WITH the conditions under which it holds
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge whether the abstract reports a limitation, failure, or negative finding, and separately whether it states the conditions that determine when the finding applies; score 0-10 for BOTH being present, low when a limitation is admitted without scope and low when scope is discussed but nothing limiting is reported.

criteria.name: Hedging-word density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how heavily the abstract hedges — 'may', 'might', 'could', 'suggests', 'potential', 'appears to', 'we believe'. Count the hedging register only, not whether the hedging is warranted.

criteria.name: Theory and experiment coupled — the experiments test the theory's own prediction
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge whether the abstract makes a theoretical claim, and separately whether the reported experiments are aimed at that claim (testing its assumptions, its predicted regime, or the instantiation it licenses) rather than at general performance; score 0-10 for the COUPLING. Score NA when neither theory nor experiment is present.

criteria.name: Explicit priority or first-ness claims
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how prominently the abstract asserts priority — 'to the best of our knowledge, the first', 'for the first time', 'we present the first study of'. Score the assertion of priority only, not whether it is true or whether the work is novel.

criteria.name: Precise delta — prior work is characterised specifically enough that the change is checkable
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge how specifically the abstract states what existing approaches actually do, and separately how specifically it states what its own contribution changes; score 0-10 for the two TOGETHER, so that a reader could verify the delta. Score low when prior work is described only as limited, insufficient, or underexplored.

criteria.name: Derivation coupling — the problem's structure is established first and the method is derived from it
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge whether the abstract establishes some structural fact about the problem (an observation, a formal property, a diagnosis) BEFORE naming its method, and separately whether the method is presented as following from that fact; score 0-10 for the two TOGETHER, low when a method is announced first and justified afterwards.

criteria.name: Generality of the formal statement TOGETHER WITH concreteness of its instantiation
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge how general the abstract's central formal or conceptual statement is, and separately how concretely it is instantiated (a specific algorithm, system, or construction that a reader could implement); score 0-10 for BOTH, low when a general statement stays abstract and low when a concrete system carries no general statement.

criteria.name: Syntactic complexity independent of total length
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how long and multi-clausal the abstract's individual SENTENCES are — subordinate clauses, parentheticals, chains of qualifiers — judged independently of how long the abstract is overall. A short abstract of tangled sentences scores high; a long abstract of short sentences scores low.

criteria.name: Rhetorical questions posed in the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses questions as a rhetorical device to frame its contribution ('Can a machine ...?', 'How can we ...?', 'This raises the question: ...'). Score the device only.

criteria.name: Restraint — claim language is calibrated BELOW what the reported results would license
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge the magnitude of what the abstract reports, and separately the strength of the language used to describe it; score 0-10 for the GAP in the understated direction — high when substantial results are described plainly and hedged appropriately, low when the language runs ahead of the evidence.

criteria.name: Non-idiomatic English and grammatical slips
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract departs from fluent idiomatic English — agreement errors, article misuse, awkward collocations, malformed constructions. Score surface fluency only, not the clarity of the underlying ideas.

criteria.name: Membership in the privacy / security / adversarial-robustness subfield
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the abstract belongs to the privacy, security, adversarial-robustness, or attack-and-defence cluster of machine learning. Score topic membership only; work of any quality in any other subfield scores 0.

criteria.name: Subsumption — prior work is exhibited as special cases of a more general statement
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the work states a general formulation and shows that existing approaches fall out of it as special cases or instances, rather than sitting alongside them as one more alternative. Score high only when the abstract names what is being subsumed.

criteria.name: Reusable artifact — what is left behind is fit for others to build on, judged scale-free
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the work leaves an artifact others could genuinely build on — a dataset, benchmark, framework, or released system — judged by its novelty, documentation, and fitness for reuse. Judge scale-free: a small, well-specified, genuinely new artifact scores HIGH and a very large but routine or undocumented one scores LOW.

criteria.name: Mechanistic explanation of an OBSERVED fact, not of the proposed method
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explains WHY some empirically observed behaviour occurs — a property of existing systems, data, or the problem — as distinct from explaining why the authors' own method works. Score NA when no empirical observation about the world is made.

criteria.name: Simplicity of the solution RELATIVE TO the difficulty of the problem it solves
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge how hard the abstract establishes its problem to be, and separately how simple the proposed solution is (few moving parts, little machinery, minimal changes to existing systems); score 0-10 for the RATIO, high when a hard problem is met with a strikingly economical solution and low when an easy problem needs elaborate machinery.

criteria.name: Names and characterises a phenomenon that did not previously have a name
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the work isolates a recurring effect or failure mode, gives it a name, and characterises it well enough that others could look for it elsewhere — as opposed to naming its own method or system.

criteria.name: Insight portability — the finding would survive replacing the specific benchmark it was shown on
criteria.instruction: Composite: judge how tied the abstract's central finding is to the particular dataset, benchmark, or system used to establish it, and separately how the finding is phrased (as a fact about the world versus a fact about a leaderboard); score 0-10 for portability, high when the finding would still mean something if the benchmark were swapped.

criteria.name: First-person narrative density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how heavily the abstract is written in the first person plural — 'we propose', 'we show', 'we find', 'our method' — as opposed to impersonal or passive construction. Count the register only.

criteria.name: Typographic emphasis used inside the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses typographic emphasis to direct attention — bold, italics, or emphasis markup around names, numbers, or claims. Score the emphasis practice only, regardless of what is emphasised.

criteria.name: Acronym density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how many distinct capitalised abbreviations the abstract introduces or uses per unit of text, counting field-standard acronyms as well as newly coined ones. Score density only.

criteria.name: Inline author-year citations inside the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how much the abstract cites prior work inline in author-year form (for example 'Smith et al., 2019') rather than referring to prior work in prose without citations. Score the citation practice only, not whether the citations are apt.
